title: The Classics Travel West
bigQuestion: What happens to a classic when it is carried into another language and culture?

story.title: Two Scholars at One Desk
story.kicker: In Hong Kong in the 1860s, a Scottish missionary and a Chinese scholar work together on the classics.
paragraphs: Hong Kong, 1863. In a study above the harbor, a Scottish missionary named James Legge rises before dawn, as he does most days. He opens the Book of Documents and a pile of Chinese commentaries. He has promised himself to translate all the major classics into English.

Beside him works Wang Tao, a Chinese scholar who had fled Shanghai after being accused of helping the Taiping rebels. Wang Tao knows the commentaries deeply. He explains hard passages, gathers notes from many editions, and argues with Legge about meanings.

Legge believes the classics must be understood on their own terms before a Westerner can judge them. His notes are long and careful. He prints the Chinese text, the English and his commentary on the same page, so readers can check his work.

In 1867 Wang Tao even travels with Legge to Scotland to continue the work. The volumes of The Chinese Classics appear from 1861 to 1872. Legge later becomes Oxford's first professor of Chinese. Wang Tao returns to Hong Kong and becomes a pioneering newspaper editor. Their translations are still read today.
story.think: Why might a translation made by two people from different cultures be stronger than one made by either alone?

sections.title: Jesuits and the First Latin Confucius

lessons.title: Matteo Ricci in China
lessons.mainIdea: The Jesuit Matteo Ricci learned classical Chinese, studied the classics and presented Christianity in terms that respected Confucian learning.
reading: *Matteo Ricci* (1552–1610) was an Italian Jesuit priest. He arrived in China in 1582 and settled in Beijing in 1601. He learned to read and write classical Chinese and dressed as a Confucian scholar.

Ricci believed that early Confucianism was compatible with Christianity. He argued that the ancient classics spoke of a supreme Lord on High (Shangdi) and that ancestor rites could be understood as honoring, not worshiping. He made friends with scholars such as Xu Guangqi, who became a Christian.

Ricci's approach is sometimes called *accommodation*: adapting to local culture. It sparked the *Chinese Rites controversy*. In 1715, Pope Clement XI ruled against allowing Chinese Christians to take part in ancestor and Confucian rites. The Kangxi emperor then restricted missionaries.

words.d: an Italian Jesuit (1552–1610) who lived in China and studied the classics
adapting a message to fit a local culture
a Catholic debate over whether Chinese Christians could keep ancestor and Confucian rites

look.title: Two Missionary Views
look.text: Missionary A: 'Honoring ancestors with bows and incense is a way of showing respect, like visiting a grave. Converts may keep it.' Missionary B: 'These are religious offerings. Converts must stop them.'
look.prompt: What was each missionary worried about? How might a Chinese Christian family have felt about the debate?

check.q: When did Matteo Ricci settle in Beijing?
check.why: Ricci arrived in China in 1582 and settled in Beijing in 1601.

check.q: What was the Chinese Rites controversy about?
choices: Whether Chinese Christians could keep ancestor and Confucian rites
check.why: Catholics debated whether converts could keep ancestor and Confucian rites.

check.q: What does 'accommodation' mean here?
choices: Adapting a message to local culture
check.why: Ricci's accommodation adapted Christian teaching to Chinese culture.

lessons.title: Confucius in Latin, 1687
lessons.mainIdea: In 1687, Jesuits in Paris published Confucius Sinarum Philosophus, the first major Western translation of Confucian classics.
reading: Jesuit scholars spent decades translating Confucian texts into *Latin*, the shared learned language of Europe. In 1687 they published *Confucius Sinarum Philosophus* (Confucius, Philosopher of the Chinese) in Paris.

The book included Latin versions of the Great Learning, the Doctrine of the Mean and the Analects, with a life of Confucius. Its editors, including Philippe Couplet and Prospero Intorcetta, presented Confucius as a wise moral philosopher who taught by natural reason.

The book shaped how Europe first saw Confucius. It also shows how *translation* carries the translator's aims. The Jesuits wanted to show that China's ancient wisdom fit with Christian belief. Later translators made different choices.

words.d: the language of learned writing in Europe for centuries
a 1687 Latin book by Jesuits presenting three of the Four Books
carrying a text from one language into another

look.title: Milestones in Western Translation
look.prompt: How many years passed between the Latin Confucius and Legge's Analects?

check.q: In what language was Confucius Sinarum Philosophus written?
check.why: The 1687 Jesuit work was in Latin.

check.q: Which texts did it include?
choices: Great Learning, Doctrine of the Mean and Analects
check.why: It presented three of the Four Books: the Great Learning, the Mean and the Analects.

check.q: What did the Jesuit editors want to show?
choices: That Confucian wisdom fit with Christian belief
check.why: The Jesuits presented Confucius as a moral philosopher compatible with Christianity.

lessons.title: Voltaire and the Enlightenment
lessons.mainIdea: Some Enlightenment thinkers, such as Voltaire and Leibniz, admired Confucius as a model of moral reason, though their picture of China was often idealized.
reading: In the 1700s, European writers of the *Enlightenment* questioned kings and church authority. Some found in Confucius a teacher of ethics based on reason rather than revelation. The philosopher Leibniz praised Chinese moral philosophy and corresponded with Jesuits in China.

*Voltaire* admired Confucius and is said to have kept his portrait in his study. He praised China as a land governed by learned officials. Some scholars see this admiration as a way to criticize France. Others note that the Enlightenment picture of China was often idealized.
By the 1800s, Western views of China had turned harsher, as European powers fought the Opium Wars. Historians study both the praise and the scorn as mirrors of Europe's own concerns.

words.d: a European movement of the 1700s stressing reason and questioning authority
a French writer (1694–1778) who admired Confucius
shown as more perfect than it really was

look.title: A Mirror, Not a Window
look.text: A French writer in 1760 praises China: 'There, the wise rule, not priests or nobles.' A British writer in 1850 says: 'China is stagnant and unchanging.' Neither writer ever visited China.
look.prompt: What might each writer really be saying about his own country? Why does it matter that neither visited?

check.q: Why did some Enlightenment thinkers admire Confucius?
choices: He taught ethics based on reason
check.why: They saw Confucian ethics as based on reason rather than revelation.

check.q: What do scholars note about the Enlightenment picture of China?
check.why: European admirers often idealized China, sometimes to criticize their own societies.

check.q: Which thinker corresponded with Jesuits in China?
check.why: Leibniz exchanged letters with Jesuits about China.

lessons.title: Legge and Wang Tao
lessons.mainIdea: James Legge, helped by Wang Tao and other Chinese scholars, translated the Chinese classics into English between 1861 and 1891.
reading: *James Legge* (1815–1897) was a Scottish missionary with the London Missionary Society. He worked in Malacca and then in Hong Kong from 1843. He decided that missionaries needed to understand the classics deeply.

His series *The Chinese Classics* appeared from 1861 to 1872. It included the Four Books, the Book of Documents, the Songs, and the Spring and Autumn with its Zuo commentary. Each page printed the Chinese text, Legge's English and extensive notes.

Legge had help. *Wang Tao* (1828–1897) contributed research on commentaries and worked with him in Hong Kong and Scotland. Scholars today stress that the translations were a joint achievement, though only Legge's name is on the title pages.

words.d: a Scottish missionary and scholar (1815–1897) who translated the Chinese classics
a Chinese scholar (1828–1897) who helped Legge and later edited newspapers
Legge's translations of the Confucian classics, 1861–1872

look.title: The Golden Rule in Legge
look.text: Tsze-kung asked, saying, 'Is there one word which may serve as a rule of practice for all one's life?' The Master said, 'Is not RECIPROCITY such a word? What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.'
look.cite: Analects 15.23, trans. James Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 1 (2nd ed., 1893)
look.prompt: Why might Legge have printed 'RECIPROCITY' in capitals? What might Western readers compare it to?

check.q: Who helped Legge with research on the commentaries?
check.why: Wang Tao worked with Legge in Hong Kong and Scotland.

check.q: What did each page of The Chinese Classics include?
check.why: Legge printed the Chinese, his translation and long notes together.

check.q: In Analects 15.23, what word does Confucius offer as a rule for life?
check.why: Legge translates the word as reciprocity: do not do to others what you do not want done to yourself.

lessons.title: Oxford and the Sacred Books
lessons.mainIdea: Legge became Oxford's first professor of Chinese and translated Confucian and Daoist texts for the Sacred Books of the East.
reading: In 1876 Legge became the first Professor of Chinese at Oxford University. He kept translating into his seventies. His students were few, but his books reached readers far beyond Oxford.

The scholar Max Müller edited a series called the *Sacred Books of the East* (1879–1910), 50 volumes of Asian religious texts in English. Legge wrote six volumes. They included the Classic of Filial Piety, the Book of Changes, the Book of Rites, and, in 1891, the Daodejing and the Zhuangzi.

Legge's translations are now in the *public domain* in the United States, so anyone may copy them. That is why this course quotes them. Scholars also note their limits: old-fashioned English, Victorian spellings like Tao Teh King and Kwang-ze, and some Christian assumptions.

words.d: a 50-volume series of Asian religious texts in English, edited by Max Müller, 1879–1910
no longer under copyright, so free for anyone to copy and use

look.title: Old and New Spellings
look.text: Legge (1891): Tao Teh King, Kwang-ze, Kung-fu-tsze, Mencius. Pinyin (today): Daodejing, Zhuangzi, Kongfuzi, Mengzi.
look.prompt: Why do the spellings differ? Why might a student need to know both?

check.q: In what year did Legge become Oxford's first Professor of Chinese?
check.why: Legge took up the Oxford chair in 1876.

check.q: Who edited the Sacred Books of the East?
check.why: Max Müller edited the 50-volume series.

check.q: Why can this course quote Legge exactly?
choices: His translations are in the U.S. public domain
check.why: Legge's 19th-century translations are no longer under copyright in the U.S.

lessons.title: A Hundred Daodejings
lessons.mainIdea: The Daodejing has been translated into English more than any other Chinese book, and each version reflects the translator's choices and aims.
reading: After Legge, English versions of the Daodejing multiplied. Scholars count well over a hundred. Some are careful scholarly translations. Others are loose *interpretations* by writers who do not read Chinese and work from earlier English versions.

Each type serves a purpose. Scholarly versions note manuscript differences, such as the Mawangdui and Guodian copies. Popular versions may speak to modern readers about calm or leadership. Critics warn that some popular versions change the meaning a great deal.
Students can compare versions carefully. Ask: Does the translator read Chinese? Which Chinese text did they use? Where do they add their own ideas? A good *citation* names the translator and year.

words.d: an explanation or free version of a text's meaning
a note that tells exactly where a quotation or idea comes from

look.title: Checking a Version
look.text: You find a Daodejing online with no translator's name. Its chapter 1 reads: 'The path to happiness cannot be put into words.' Legge's ch. 1 reads: 'The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao.'
look.prompt: What questions would you ask about the online version before quoting it in a report?

check.q: Why do Daodejing versions differ so much?
choices: Each reflects the translator's choices and aims
check.why: Translators choose words, sources and aims differently.

check.q: What should a good citation name?
check.why: A citation names the translator and year so readers can check.

check.q: What do critics warn about some popular versions?
choices: They may change the meaning a great deal
check.why: Some popular versions by non-readers of Chinese depart far from the text.

lessons.title: Emerson, Thoreau and the Dial
lessons.mainIdea: American writers of the 1800s, such as Emerson and Thoreau, read and quoted Confucian sayings from early translations.
reading: In the 1840s, the New England writers called *Transcendentalists* read Asian texts in translation. Their magazine, *The Dial*, printed selections of Confucian sayings in 1843. Ralph Waldo Emerson admired Confucius as a moral teacher.
Henry David Thoreau quoted Confucius several times in *Walden* (1854). He drew on the Analects and the Great Learning to support his ideas about simple living and self-improvement.
These writers read the classics through their own interests. Historians note they often mixed Confucian, Hindu and Buddhist sources. Still, they introduced many Americans to Chinese thought.

words.d: a group of New England writers in the 1800s, including Emerson and Thoreau
Thoreau's 1854 book about simple living, which quotes Confucius

look.title: Borrowing a Voice
look.text: A writer in Massachusetts in 1850 quotes Confucius on self-improvement in a book about living alone by a pond. He does not read Chinese. He found the quotation in an English translation.
look.prompt: What might this writer gain by quoting Confucius? What might he miss?

check.q: Which magazine printed Confucian sayings in 1843?
check.why: The Transcendentalist magazine The Dial printed Confucian selections in 1843.

check.q: Which book by Thoreau quotes Confucius?
check.why: Thoreau's Walden (1854) quotes Confucius several times.

check.q: What do historians note about the Transcendentalists' reading?
choices: They mixed sources and read through their own interests
check.why: They often blended Confucian, Hindu and Buddhist sources for their own ideas.

lessons.title: Exclusion and Community
lessons.mainIdea: While Americans read Chinese classics, the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 barred most Chinese laborers from entering the United States.
reading: Chinese immigrants came to the United States in large numbers from the 1850s. They worked in gold mines, built the western part of the first transcontinental railroad, and opened businesses. Many faced violence and unfair laws.

In 1882 Congress passed the *Chinese Exclusion Act*. It barred most Chinese laborers from immigrating and blocked Chinese immigrants from becoming citizens. It was the first U.S. law to ban immigration by a specific national group. It was repealed in 1943.

Chinese Americans built communities anyway, including Chicago's Chinatown. Families kept festivals, temples, churches and family associations. Historians note the *irony*: the same years that Americans praised Confucius, Chinese people were shut out.

words.d: an 1882 U.S. law that barred most Chinese laborers from immigrating; repealed in 1943
a contrast between what is expected or praised and what actually happens
a person who moves to a new country to live

choices: Barred most Chinese laborers from immigrating
check.why: The 1882 act barred most Chinese laborers and blocked citizenship.

check.q: When was the Exclusion Act repealed?
check.why: Congress repealed the Exclusion Act in 1943.

check.q: What irony do historians note?
choices: Americans praised Confucius while shutting out Chinese people
check.why: Praise for Chinese wisdom coexisted with laws excluding Chinese immigrants.

lessons.title: The Classics in Classrooms Today
lessons.mainIdea: Today the Chinese classics are studied in American schools and universities as philosophy, literature and history, alongside living communities who keep them.
reading: Today, American students may read the Analects or the Daodejing in world history, philosophy or literature classes. Universities teach classical Chinese. Scholars compare Confucian ethics with Aristotle, and Daoist ideas with other traditions.

Students also learn from living communities. Chinese American, Korean American and Vietnamese American families keep festivals and values linked to the classics. Some families are Christian, Buddhist or have no religion, and still honor Confucian ideals of family and learning.

Studying the classics well means using good *sources*, naming translations, and attributing ideas. It also means listening to the many people, in Asia and in America, for whom these books are part of their *heritage*.

words.d: traditions, beliefs and objects passed down from earlier generations
a text or person that information comes from

look.title: A Class Discussion
look.text: In a Chicago classroom, students read Analects 15.23. One says: 'This is like the Golden Rule.' Another, whose grandmother is from Guangzhou, says: 'My family says this at dinner.' A third asks: 'Is it the same idea, or just similar?'
look.prompt: How does each student add to the discussion? How could the class answer the third question carefully?

check.q: In which subjects might American students study the classics?
check.why: The classics are studied as philosophy, literature and history.

check.q: Which is an example of studying the classics well?

check.why: Good study names sources and attributes beliefs.

check.q: What does 'heritage' mean?
choices: Traditions passed down from earlier generations
check.why: Heritage is what is passed down from earlier generations.
